title: How To Turn Around Difficult Students With A Simple Psychological Trick
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin distinguishes his recommended strategy from manipulative behavior-management tactics like PBIS by explaining that the 'trick' here is one teachers play on themselves, not on students. He grounds the piece in the Pygmalion effect (subconscious positive expectations raise others' performance) and its inverse, the Golem effect, arguing that difficult students carry negative labels imprinted by years of subtle signals from adults — lectures, false praise, extra chances — that communicate low expectations regardless of what adults say aloud. His proposed fix is twofold: first, apply the core SCM classroom-management approach to bring a difficult student to behavioral equilibrium; second, consciously choose to believe, in both behavior and inner conviction, that your most challenging student is actually your best student, so your micro-expressions and mannerisms transmit a new, positive Pygmalion signal instead of reinforcing the old Golem one. The article's throughline is that changing a difficult student's behavior starts with the teacher changing how they privately see that student.
points: The Pygmalion effect: a person's subconscious expectations of someone, expressed through tone, expression, and behavior, cause the other person to rise or fall to meet them.
Difficult students carry a negative 'Golem effect' label built up from years of lectures, extra chances, and false praise that communicate low expectations no matter what's said aloud.
The 'trick' is not manipulating students — it's consciously pretending, in both behavior and genuine inner belief, that your most challenging students are your best ones.
Once a difficult student reaches behavioral equilibrium through consistent classroom management, their old 'difficult' label can start to fall away like snake skin.
The change in the teacher's private perception of a student must come before any change in the student's behavior.
quotes: The Pygmalion effect is the name given to the phenomenon, proven many decades ago, that our subconscious beliefs and expectations of others affect their behavior.
Unfortunately, the opposite is also true. Often called the Golem effect, if your boss expects you to fail, then it’s an uphill battle to overcome the prophecy you’ve been saddled with.

All the lectures, talking-tos, behavior contracts, extra chances, appeasements, rewards, sighs, false praise, and hundreds of constant subconscious mannerisms communicate loud and clear to these students that they’re not good enough.
The way it works is that you’re going to pretend, in both your behavior and how you feel and believe on the inside, that your most challenging students are actually your best students.
Your expectations will be of good behavior and hard work, which they’ll receive and seek to meet without you having to say a word.
